#10017. PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.

James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending. Shira's path into the industry was, as he puts it, as "consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow." Originally considering a career in law, Shira decided to pivot, more seriously considering pursuing cybersecurity through independent study, and then formal education. Today, he oversees both technology and security at one of the world's largest professional services firms, giving him a broad perspective on the challenges facing security leaders.

In this episode of Heard It From a CISO with Dark Reading associate editor Kristina Beek, Shira discusses the skills and experience needed to build a career in cybersecurity, including the value of industry certifications, higher education, and on-the-job experience. He also examines the qualities that distinguish effective security teams, the challenges of balancing the CISO and CIO roles, and how security leaders can establish credibility with corporate boards. For Shira, successful leadership comes down to more than technical expertise. It involves building trust, communicating complex issues clearly, and creating an environment where employees can develop.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Shira also shares his thoughts on the topic on everyone's minds: artificial intelligence. He warns that rapid adoption is expanding attack surfaces, adding pressure on security teams, but also notes that AI technology will add opportunities for professionals seeking roles in the field. As for what's ahead, Shira expects significant societal and industry change and shares that this rate of change is likely to be the new standard — it’s best if everyone is prepared to go along for the ride.

This is part of Dark Reading's ongoing Heard It From a CISO video series, which features frank, exclusive conversations with cybersecurity leaders in the trenches. Check out the entire series here.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

James Shira: I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times. But I think that makes for better decisions.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Dark Reading's Kristina Beek: Hi, everyone. My name is Kristina Beek. I'm an associate editor at Dark Reading, and I'm here for another episode of Heard It From a CISO. Today, I'm joined by James Shira. Thank you so much for joining us. I would love it if you could introduce yourself and talk about your background and your current role as CISO at PwC.

James Shira: Sure. It's great to be with you today. My name is James. I am the global CISO and CIO for PwC. I've been involved in what we used to call IT security since 1999. I became a CISO in the early 2000s, I think 2000 or 2001, really based on an opportunity and happenstance. I've been involved in the community since that time, now 25 or 26 years. For the last eight years, I've also been operating as our global CIO.

DR's Kristina Beek: Love to hear that. How did you first get involved specifically in cybersecurity, technology, or security in general? I know there are a lot of different ways people get involved. Some people study computer science, and some come from very alternative backgrounds. What does your path look like?

James Shira: I think my path is probably as consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow. I was planning on getting a degree to become a lawyer, actually. Then, being a blue-collar kid, I realized I couldn't afford law school. After two years, I needed to make a change, so I redirected toward business and information systems. That was my undergraduate background.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

When I graduated in 1998, there was a bit of a mini-recession, what we often refer to as the dot-com crash. At the time, I used to read the physical Wall Street Journal pretty religiously, and there was a lot of discussion about security. We didn't call it cyber then. I figured this was a space that needed leaders and leadership. I was very interested in working toward and building an executive career path, and I wasn't sure — probably like a lot of college graduates — how to go from having no experience to having an opportunity to be in a role like the ones I'm privileged to have today.

I really started by researching, reading, learning, and studying, a lot of self-directed study, including some computer science-based material. I also did a program at Columbia that's now a master's program, which was very helpful to me. I was one of the first students when we started. The idea was like an MBA for technologists, and I'm proud to say it's now a Master of Science degree. I had the opportunity to be a student mentor there for a long time. It was really on a whim that I thought this space was going to be incredibly interesting, and it's proven to be.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to my next question: What would you recommend to somebody who wants to go into cybersecurity today? In general, what would your advice be? What insights could you provide in terms of what would be best to study? Should they prioritize certifications or a four-year education? There are a lot of different ways to go into cybersecurity today.

James Shira: For sure. I think the four-year education discussion we're all having right now is really relevant. I have younger kids, so I've got some time before they get there. I think it's a really relevant conversation because of the cost. Having worked my way through college and taken out loans at the time, those loan amounts look really small compared with what people are confronted with today. I think it's a very fair question and debate that people should have.

I'm a big proponent of certification on our security team. We really encourage people to do it, and we sponsor some of them. I'm not going to name them because we'd be here for a long time, but I think it's a very smart strategy.

The way I describe it to our folks is that I talk about the concepts of internal equity and external equity. Your internal equity when you come out of college is zero. You're new; you're coming into the industry. You build that up over time with your employer. Obviously, you want to pick the right place to work, as best you can. In the early days, experience in and of itself is the value you're pursuing.

The second piece, external equity, is something you can drive as hard as you want. As a young person without a lot of experience, you can pursue certifications. Some require years of work, but there's a lot out there. The most successful people I've had the privilege to mentor start out with a high degree of emphasis on certifications. Then, after five to seven years of experience, they make a choice about whether they're going to pursue a management track or a higher-end technical director or subject-matter-expert track.

On your question about a four-year education versus certifications, my personal view is that if you want to be in a role similar to mine, or the same as mine, you're going to want that four-year degree. You may even want a master's eventually. If that's your intended path, I would encourage you, notwithstanding the loans, to complete your undergraduate degree. There are a lot of great schools with programs that can be helpful. If you look at that and say to yourself, "That's a significant debt burden, and I don't think it makes sense. I'm not sure I want to pursue being an executive," then I think you should do the certifications and work on getting as much experience as you can.

DR's Kristina Beek: That's a great insight. You talked about building equity and how, when you're fresh out of college, that really depends on your employer and the company you choose to work for. Moving back to PwC, what interested you in the company? Why did you choose to work there, and what has it been like being CISO?

James Shira: When I was coming out of Zurich Financial Services, now Zurich Insurance Group — which was also a great time in my career — I was interested in finding the right CISO challenge at a similar or bigger scale. What interested me about PwC at that time was that it was a 160-plus-year-old institution. I had never worked in professional services; I had only worked in financial services. So a different industry interested me.

I think the organization's values here at PwC were very consistent with mine, and it's been a privilege to be here. It sounds clichéd, but it's really a great place. The quality of people, on average, in my experience, has been really high. People have a desire to do the right thing, and as a CISO, that's incredibly helpful. A lot of our security strategy is culturally centered on employee behavior and training, so those things were very consistent and have been very helpful.

I know some CISOs drive programs through cultures that are less amenable. This culture was incredibly amenable to moving its security program to the next level. Nobody's program is perfect, but that was helpful. Lastly, I had the opportunity to bring a lot of my colleagues with me. I have the privilege of sitting in these roles, but it's not something I did on my own. It's something we've done collectively as a team. Given the scale of the mission here, I had the opportunity to bring some colleagues from my previous employer over, and it's been awesome to see their careers flourish here as well. In short, it's a great place to work.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to a follow-up question. When it comes to a team, whether it's business-oriented or security-focused, what makes a great team? What kinds of people are you looking for, whether in terms of personality or skills?

James Shira: I'm going to answer your question in reverse order. The people I like to work with don't come in a common package. I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times, but I think that makes for better decisions.

The people I'm looking for don't have to have gone to a specific school. They don't necessarily need a traditional profile, but they definitely need to be self-confident and self-directed. I talk to the team a lot about emotional resiliency. I think it's a really important concept in the security industry because, when I got started, security was past the mailroom, past the bathrooms, in the basement somewhere, and rarely in the boardroom. Now, people coming into the field wouldn't even recognize that, because security is such a central, strategically critical issue for companies. I need that confidence in our employees so that, when they become the leaders they can be, they can flourish based on that confidence. It's hard to build a great team without that.

The second piece I think is incredibly important is transparency. It's something I work diligently to practice when I'm speaking in front of the thousands of colleagues I have the privilege of leading: being as brutally transparent as possible about whatever we're trying to do. It's uncomfortable at times, and it can be challenging to answer the questions you get, but I think it provokes the kind of cultural engagement that makes for a great team.

The one thing I'll say lastly is that I don't think mediocrity, as a rule, fits in high-performing teams. You have to embrace your high performers, try to elevate and promote them, and create an environment where they can be as self-directed and successful as they can be.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. When you were answering that, one of the things you talked about was how the CISO role and cybersecurity in general are now in the boardroom. I see a lot of articles about how to communicate with C-suite members as a CISO, how to deal with friction, and how to get your board to believe you. What would you say about communicating your needs as a CISO to the rest of the board? Do you encounter friction in your experience, and how do you deal with that?

James Shira: I think it's a great question. I'm going to offer a point of view. I'll start by saying I've gotten it wrong. I don't have all the answers, but I've learned through mistakes and by having great mentors.

I think credibility with a board starts, frankly, through delivery. The first thing you have to do is build a track record as best you can. That might sound counterintuitive: Don't I need the board's buy-in before I deliver? Somewhat, but I think conversations with our various boards here, and the conversations I've had previously, show that over time, through delivery of the program and driving the change you're advocating for, you can build a lot of credibility.

The second of my three points is that you have to find your own authentic voice. Personally, I'm not a natural. I kind of joke with the team at times that I'm a radio guy, not a TV guy, and I've had to work at being a TV guy. You have to find your own authenticity through your own style. A lot of times, those of us who get the privilege of being in these C-level jobs receive a lot of advice and pressure about how to present and who to be. I would encourage people listening to find their own style and approach that works best for them. Obviously, measure it against how effective it is, but embrace the style that's authentic to you. For me, I just try to be myself with our board.

The last thing I'd say, and I think it's maybe the most important point, is that you have to bring the expertise to the board, not try to drag the board to your expertise. In our domain, don't underestimate how intimidating it can be for the people listening. It's security. They see the headlines. Maybe an issue has occurred in that business. As board members, they feel responsible for providing oversight over management, and they're under tremendous pressure to do so. Don't underestimate that.

If you come at them with a high degree of expertise, terms, acronyms, and things they don't understand, I've found that doesn't work. That would be one of the mistakes I've made in the past. What's worked well for me is not to dumb it down, but to simplify it. If you have enough mastery of a topic, you can describe it in a way that doesn't make the other person feel intimidated and helps them say, "OK, I get that." One suggestion I would offer is to use storytelling. That's what I've done, and it has worked well for me.

DR's Kristina Beek: While you're obviously CISO, you're also CIO, so you have two perspectives. What is it like balancing the responsibilities of both roles?

James Shira: The good news is that, over the last eight years I've had the privilege of being in these roles, there's been a tremendous amount of harmonization between the technology transformation of large enterprises and the need to get the cyber piece right. Therefore, unlike when I started, when security was past the mailroom and in the basement, it's now such a primary issue for organizations that it's really on the CIO's agenda. I think having both of those skill sets is a very critical thing in this day and age.

The one difference I'd acknowledge for the audience, because otherwise anybody watching would think I missed it, is that at times the CIO role can be inherently more political than the CISO role. Let me explain briefly. As a CISO, you objectively know what good looks like: Don't have a breach, don't have an incident, improve your audit posture, drive good risk management, and so on. What good looks like in the CIO world can sometimes be less black and white and more gray. It can change in a way that a traditional CISO might find challenging to navigate.

I, for one, never anticipated the amount of passion and energy that debating different HR or finance platforms might bring. I've learned how to spend a lot of time with CFOs and COOs in our businesses. That's made me not only better professionally, but also more sympathetic to the issues they have, especially in some of the smaller businesses where a decision we might make from a CIO perspective has a significant material impact on their cost basis. There are differences, but in summary, it's a very complementary experience for me. The biggest challenge is time management and moving time between the different things.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. AI is, of course, always part of the conversation. It's changing how attackers work, and it's also changing how organizations operate. What do you see as the biggest cybersecurity opportunity or risk associated with AI right now?

James Shira: I think the most important issue with AI, straight down the middle, is how it changes, evolves, and increases an organization's attack surface. The second issue is the rate of change it brings: how fast it moves and how fast systems have to move. Those are the two dynamics.

What happens to the size of your attack surface? AI can really explode it. At the same time, AI puts pressure on the pace of change across the whole security function. For us specifically, that means dealing with the amount of patching, vulnerability management, inbound requests, and client requests. You have to manage those two dynamics.

On the technology front, in my career — which some people in this audience might think is long, while others might think it's not that long yet — I've never seen anything move as fast. In a short period of time, we've gone from a nascent technology that we're all excited about to actually operationalizing it. At least in my career, I haven't seen anything cross that divide so quickly. Therefore, I think it's ultimately the biggest change-management exercise, maybe ever. That's really where leaders need to center and focus their time.

DR's Kristina Beek: A lot of people are coming out of college or going into college with the expectation of going into cybersecurity or computer science. AI is changing the field very rapidly. A lot of people are scared that they may not even have a job or that there may not be a place for them in this field. What would you say to that, with the rise of AI?

James Shira: I understand where people get that. I understand how people get that. I think it's understandable, but I think it's wrong. The amount of change across society and industries is significant. It's very difficult for me to chart a course in my head for what isn't going to change. Therefore, I think the opportunity for young professionals is to be the change agents — to deliver the change.

I think one thing we don't always do well for our young professionals, but need to, is tell them the truth about the adversity of change management. It's hard. It's hard, and it's going to be hard for them. Do I think AI is a job-elimination technology? I don't. But I understand and respect how people might reach that conclusion.

If you're doing highly repetitive, data-centric activities, that's not, frankly, what you go to college for. Some of us had to do that coming out of college, earning our stripes, but that's not generally what you go to college for. That probably gets changed a lot by AI. Of course. I don't think it's a displacement strategy.

DR's Kristina Beek: Going back to what you said about how AI is changing things so rapidly, what do you think cybersecurity leaders will spend the most time thinking about three to five years from now? I know that's hard because things are changing so quickly, but what do you see for the future?

James Shira: I think the constants I would expect not to go away are the rate of change, the pace, and the pressure. Therefore, I think you have to find consistency in process and strategic principles, meaning how you manage your strategy shouldn't change. You should find the things in executing the strategy and operationalizing it that don't need to change, because so much around you will be changing.

In our history, and in at least my part of the 20-year history of IT security and cybersecurity, when there's been a technical change — think cloud, client-server, mobile, or whatever — we've effectively changed every aspect of how we implemented security controls. I'm hoping and working diligently to avoid repeating that pattern in the AI space because I think it just adds too much volume to an already high-intensity, high-volume situation.

Three to five years from now, I'm hoping AI can be a much more consistent enabler of delivering secure outcomes, but we're still learning how to fully operationalize it. Then there's the issue of token costs, which we're not going to get into today, but that has a high degree of relationship to driving the overall security budget, which we're figuring out as we go.

Secondly, I don't think most companies will have enough money to build a security program the way we've historically done it, at the size and scale that AI could imply would be required. Third, I think organizations are going to have to shrink their digital footprint as they transform. The good news is that — obviously, hope is not a strategy — AI will hopefully allow us to interact with our systems of state much more efficiently than building applications as the recurring front door to all of our systems, as we've done for the last 10 or 20 years. That ought to have a great benefit in reducing the attack surface, too. I think that's what companies need to do, and I think that's what will look so different in three to five years.

Lastly, I'd say I'm expecting significant societal and industry change, especially in a five-year window. I'm not sure I'm going to have a robot at home, but maybe some of us will. I think physical AI is going to place a significant premium on investment capacity, both on the hardware side and on the adoption and implementation side.

There are Orwellian views of that, where you could see the doom and gloom. I think there's also a tremendous opportunity. Some countries are not having the birth rates we need. Frankly, there isn't enough reproduction to maintain the number of people in society. So robots in some places in the world are going to be incredibly helpful in allowing us to deliver the things people need in society.

But I'm excited by it. I'll summarize by saying I think the big fundamental choice you have to make every morning when you wake up is to embrace the change, both in yourself and in how you do the job, because the change is almost — I joked with a colleague the other day, and she's a really capable runner while I am not, that this is kind of like being on the treadmill at the speed Annie would go at, not the speed James would go at. Some days I feel like I'm hanging in there, and other days I feel like I'm about to fall off the back of the treadmill. I think everybody just needs to say that's part of this.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. That's great to hear. Normally, I end these interviews by asking what the future of cybersecurity looks like to you, but we've already touched on that. So I'd rather end with a different question: You've spent a lot of time in tech and security and have seen how it's evolved. What has been the most rewarding part of that work, and what do you think will continue to challenge or motivate you, especially in a field where the risks are sometimes really high?

James Shira: Sure. It's an easy answer for me: It's the people part. It's the team. Every success I've had the privilege of being part of is not a James thing. I had a role, sure, but it's a team thing.

When you see someone — we have a number of people in our organization who started as interns at my previous employer. One colleague started as an intern and is now an executive. Another colleague, Annie, whom I mentioned, is now a partner. Those are the things that lift me back up when I have a bad day, which happens. It's when we see people building and shining in their own way, self-actualizing. That's pretty cool, and I think that's the right way things should work.

Look, it doesn't always work that way. There are probably people on the team who don't feel they got a fair chance, or who feel something didn't go perfectly. That's the challenge of working in teams of people, because people — me, you, all of us — are not perfect.

But the best days for me are when I see colleagues rise, shine, and do great things, and even leave the organization and go do great things somewhere else. That's pretty awesome. I think that's our opportunity with AI and security. We have to embrace it, try to see the positive in it, and grow through it.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. I so enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much for joining me today.

James Shira: Me too. Thanks for your time.

#10016. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 3): Attention is all you profile

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:

The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace shows the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

From the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that issue and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:

So attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

Before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:

Figure 1 shows the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the new operations are easy to spot:

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually launched.

Figure 2 shows the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

The in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up quickly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

Out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

We just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:

This one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:

Normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) shows why the alarm bells ring, the math backend launches 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 launched with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

In Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?"

The kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

In the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:

On the GPU this shows up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):

A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

Put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend launches only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

This is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

Let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

FlashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

Here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

Blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

If you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

And that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

By now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

Flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

No transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

It launches through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

The "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the plan (the "knob" search) on every call.

Fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

On the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

State out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

Profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗

Thanks to Noe Flandre for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

The blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗

Thanks for the series, really delightful!

#10015. Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident'

Market research company brings in external specialists to grok cause and scope

Market research giant Ipsos says it's currently investigating a "cybersecurity incident," and has reported the matter to the authorities.

In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company  confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal investigation is ongoing.

"Upon discovery, we promptly activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident, and engaged external cybersecurity specialists to support our investigation," it said [PDF].

"The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident. We have reported the matter to the relevant authorities."

Ipsos confirmed the attack had no impact on its operations or customer service delivery, however, it did not comment on the nature of the attack or whether any data was compromised.

"We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously," Ipsos added. "Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly.

"As the investigation is ongoing, we are not in a position to comment further at this stage."

The company declined our requests for additional data, as it does not want to release unverified information to the market.

Founded in France in 1975, Ipsos is one of the leading market research companies in the world, employing nearly 20,000 people and operating in 220 cities across 90 markets.

It is routinely engaged by businesses for its market research data, as well as by public sector organizations for its opinion polling, often responsible for providing data regarding political views and satisfaction surveys.

Tasked with procuring a wealth of data on myriad topics, Ipsos also offers data analytics services that turn the information it gathers through research, polls, and surveys into insights that inform organizations' business strategies. ®

#10014. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#10013. Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics

Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.

To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon showed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it plans the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.

Hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.

A fast, capable model is only half the story. Building a robot application has always meant gluing together drivers, calibration scripts, simulators, perception code, and a UI, which requires robotics expertise and a lot of time. The new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity packages that work into skills Gemini can use on your behalf:

This allows you to build and preview high-quality simulated scenes and assets—whether described, imported from links/documents, or uploaded via workspace photos—right alongside your code. #10012. Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

#10011. REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant

Amazon shunts some real estate off its books, a move Omdia analyst says may be about economics, as AI buildout weighs on hyperscaler finances

Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years.

Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion.

AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis. This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs.

A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them.

One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi.

We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed.

In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build."

AWS does lease capacity from other datacenter operators, of course, and has existing agreements with partners like STACK Infrastructure to develop $12 billion worth of campus sites across northwest Louisiana, signed earlier this year.

Sale-leaseback transactions are not unheard of in the datacenter industry. QTS Realty Trust (also backed by Blackstone) developed facilities for lease by Microsoft, for example.

BXDC is a real estate investment trust (REIT), launched by Blackstone on the New York Stock Exchange earlier this year. The AWS deal is its first since then.

"We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation," says its president and CEO Nick Pell.

"The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders."

Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building Alan Howard says that decisions to lease or own are always a math problem in terms of the economics.

"I'm not sure those datacenter assets bring much benefit to their financials sitting on their balance sheet and it's possible a sale/leaseback is more economical. Keep in mind that all this has nothing to do with all the IT equipment inside, rather just the building and its infrastructure," he told The Register.

"It's also clear that the massive capex spending by hyperscalers is putting pressure on their financials and they are leaning on debt markets to fund some of the buildout. Of course, using debt is not out of the ordinary, but I imagine the debt for AI buildout is significantly more now than in the past."

The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to certain closing conditions. According to the Form 8-K, the agreement can be terminated by either party if it isn't closed by December 31, 2026, with the non-breaching party entitled to a termination fee of $150 million. ®

#10010. AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesThe new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL.

How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!
